questions.prompt: Which Millbrook component is the central workstation used to reach several building systems?

options.text: BMS-WS, the building-management workstation
MGAS-PANEL, the medical-gas alarm
LIFT-CTRL, the lift controller
AHU-OT1, a theatre air-handling unit

questions.explanation: The chapter names BMS-WS as the central workstation through which several building systems can be reached; the other items are controlled systems or alarms.

questions.prompt: Why does networking an air-handling controller make it a cyber-physical security concern?

options.text: It automatically removes the need for facilities staff
A remote command can change physical equipment and clinical conditions
It changes only digital records, never the physical environment
It proves that the controller has already been compromised

questions.explanation: A networked controller can turn a screen command into a physical actuator change. Reachability creates a security concern without proving that any compromise occurred.

questions.prompt: What is the most relevant patient-safety consequence of losing positive pressure in an operating theatre?

options.text: A slower office email service
A louder ventilation fan
Unfiltered air may enter, raising surgical infection risk
The hospital automatically loses all network access

questions.explanation: The book links theatre positive-pressure loss to unfiltered air entering the room, possible infection, and postponement of surgery.

questions.prompt: If the medical-gas alarm is silenced during an actual oxygen-pressure drop, what is the immediate decision risk?

options.text: The alarm becomes easier to maintain
The oxygen supply rises automatically
The lift controller stops by design
Staff may remain unaware and respond too late for patients

questions.explanation: The clinical danger is lost warning: staff may not learn of the real supply fault in time to protect patients receiving oxygen.

questions.prompt: Why should Aisha meet the estates manager early in the Millbrook case?

options.text: Estates operates the BMS and manages building-system contractors
Estates replaces every clinical decision maker
IT security is forbidden to document building systems
Contractor access needs no named owner

questions.explanation: The estates team operates the building-management system and holds contractor relationships, so it is essential for an agreed ownership map.

questions.prompt: Which result best closes the building-system ownership gap described in the chapter?

options.text: A spreadsheet of devices without responsible people
One named owner per system, agreed by estates and IT security
An assumption that every contractor owns all hospital risk
A decision to postpone responsibility until an incident

questions.explanation: The worked case calls for a short, jointly accepted list with one named owner for each system so findings do not stall between teams.

questions.prompt: Which comparison matches the chapter's distinction between office IT and hospital building systems?

options.text: Both can only delay paperwork
Building systems cannot affect patients directly
Office IT failures may delay work; building-system failures may harm patients
Office IT always presents greater clinical danger

questions.explanation: The text contrasts ordinary work delay with physical consequences such as infection risk, lost gas alarms, and delayed patient transfer.

questions.prompt: What additional information makes a consequence statement useful for prioritizing building-system risks?

options.text: The workstation wallpaper color
Only the vendor's marketing label
The number of security acronyms in the report
How long the hospital can cope before harm becomes likely

questions.explanation: The chapter asks for a clinically recognizable consequence and its timescale. The time before likely harm informs later planning and incident priorities.

questions.prompt: How should a reader treat Millbrook Hospital and Aisha Bello in the worked example?

options.text: As synthetic teaching examples, not a reported real incident
As verified public hospital records
As a source of authorization to test real systems
As evidence that all hospitals use identical equipment

questions.explanation: The book explicitly labels Millbrook, Aisha and the case figures as invented; they illustrate reasoning and authorize no real-system access.
questions.source: Chapter 1, Worked example and educational boundary

questions.prompt: Before treating an analyst's predicted patient consequence as confirmed, whose input is needed?

options.text: Only the analyst's own second guess
Clinical and estates staff familiar with the system
A public search result about an unrelated hospital
Any contractor without the hospital's involvement

questions.explanation: The chapter's limitation states that the analyst's guess is only a starting point; clinical and estates staff must confirm the consequence.
